soil-fert-034.title: Using finished compost on fields and in beds
soil-fert-034.text:
A field needs only a thin dusting of compost, about 6 mm (0.24 in). Compost applied is finished compost used on fields, in beds and in growing mixes to add organic matter and nutrients (see {{ref:soil-fert-028}}). On open fields it is broadcast in that thin layer and worked in before planting. A layer of 25 mm (0.98 in) or more is used to rebuild poor soils or control erosion. Added to soil, coir or peat, it improves tilth and supplies humus and nutrients. Tilled in, it raises organic matter and overall fertility.

Compost is rarely used alone. It is mixed with sand, grit, bark, vermiculite, perlite or clay granules, and blends of 20-30% compost are common for transplanting seedlings. Seeding directly into compost is not advised: it dries fast, immature compost may hold germination-inhibiting phytotoxins, and undecomposed lignin may tie up nitrogen. Ready compost is dark brown or black with an earthy smell, and it can increase plant immunity to diseases and pests.

Finished compost supplies little readily available nitrogen, since composting converts much N to stable organic forms while P and K availability is unchanged. It still releases other nutrients slowly and raises organic matter. Annual high rates set by nitrogen need overload soil with phosphorus and potassium, and salts may build up under high tunnels and greenhouses. Soil tests should guide a switch to legume cover crops.

soil-fert-253.title: Management intensive grazing: many paddocks, short stays
soil-fert-253.text:
Pastures grazed continuously produce poorly. Repeated grazing of early regrowth depletes root reserves and weakens plants. Management intensive grazing rotates animals through many paddocks and does not regraze one until its plants have regrown. Cycles run from about a week or 10 days up to 6-8 weeks depending on season and weather, and dairy cows may get a fresh paddock after every milking. Harvesting and fertilizing need little equipment or labour, and electric fencing makes new paddocks quick to set up. Intensively managed pasture often lowers production cost despite the animals' foraging energy.

Well-managed pasture combines perennial forage, no tillage and regular manure. New York soil health scores for organic matter, active carbon, respiration, water capacity and aggregate stability were far higher under pasture ({{ref:soil-found-045}}). Stocking can reach about 100,000 pounds of animals per acre for 8-12 hours, used to suppress or kill poor plant species and let hooves help reseed more productive ones. Where animals roam large rangeland by day and are stocked densely at night, the carbon, nutrients and seeds they gather are excreted into the small area, boosting fertility and revegetation.

Grazing crop residue after grain harvest cuts feed costs and improves nutrient and carbon cycling. Cattle grazing corn residue in winter on the Great Plains raised soil health and yields. Swath grazing leaves annual crops such as barley and triticale cut in swaths for beef cattle, which improves forage access under deep snow.

soil-fert-239.title: When farms specialize, the nutrient cycle breaks
soil-fert-239.text:
Specialized crop-only and animal-only farms break the nutrient cycle, causing excess on one and depletion on the other. Animal operations such as CAFOs often import feed from afar, so the supplying crop farms need large fertilizer amounts to replace the exported nutrients. Manure piling up relative to the land base can be applied beyond crop needs, polluting ground and surface water. Stored manure ({{ref:soil-fert-023}}) can contaminate surface water directly.

Animals excrete most of the nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in their feed, so animal-product farms export few nutrients, whereas annual grain and vegetable farms export many. Annual-only farms have little reason to grow perennial forages. Growing only one or two annuals complicates weed control, forgoes multi-year grass and legume soil health, favours pests and demands much nitrogen fertilizer. Integrating livestock can make a farm more sustainable but more complex, and done wrongly it can add environmental problems.

soil-fert-263.title: Nitrogen and phosphorus: two nutrients, opposite habits
soil-fert-263.text:
Nitrogen moves; phosphorus mostly stays put. That contrast shapes how each is supplied, lost and managed. Nitrogen comes mainly from decomposing organic matter and can be added biologically by legumes ({{ref:soil-fert-099}}, {{ref:soil-fert-127}}). No biological process adds phosphorus, which also comes from soil minerals. Nitrate, the main form plants absorb, is very mobile. Phosphorus movement is very limited, and its available form is a small dissolved amount, mainly H2PO4- and HPO4 2-.

Most N loss is nitrate leaching, denitrification or ammonia volatilization. Leaching dominates in sandy soils and denitrification in heavy loams and clays. Phosphorus is lost mainly in runoff and eroded sediment, but low losses have a high effect per unit on water quality because P often limits freshwater algae. P leaching matters in artificially drained fields: after years of excess manure or compost, P-saturated sandy soils leak P, and liquid manure can flow through wormholes and cracks to drain lines.

Cover crops store nitrogen that would otherwise leach, and mobilize P through mycorrhizae and store it for the next crop. Excess N pollutes water with nitrate, raises nitrous oxide from denitrification, wastes energy in manufacture, speeds loss of soil organic matter and is linked to more insect damage. Making, hauling and applying N fertilizer ({{ref:soil-fert-007}}) is about 30 percent of the energy used to grow corn.

soil-fert-262.title: Composting: what it gains and when to skip it
soil-fert-262.text:
Composted material is less bulky than the feedstock, so it is cheaper to transport and nicer to handle. The pile shrinks by 30-60 percent as carbon dioxide and water escape. Heat kills many weed seeds and pathogens, odors and flies decline, and compost has about half the bulk and weight of manure. Composting removes the nitrogen drawdown that follows adding sawdust or straw to soil, reduces nutrient solubility and stream pollution, and helps lower antibiotic levels in manure.

Compost stores easily for application when conditions are right. It lets farms with excess manure move nutrients to fields, gardens and landscapes that need them.

Direct addition of residues can be better. Fresh residues stimulate more aggregate-binding gums, supply more readily available nutrients and cost less labour and energy. Composting suits hard-to-handle, unsafe or odorous feedstocks, long hauls, pathogen concerns or good markets.

soil-fert-270.title: Managing nitrogen and phosphorus: count, test, time, place, cover
soil-fert-270.text:
Nitrogen and phosphorus behave differently in soil ({{ref:soil-fert-263}}), yet they need similar management. Take all nutrient sources into account, using soil, manure and compost tests, crop residue N, and the 4R principles of right rate, time, place and source, plus conservation practices. Place fertilizer below the surface, split N applications where leaching or denitrification threaten, and apply when leaching and runoff threats are minimal.

Cover crops with minimal or no tillage improve structure, cut leaching, runoff and denitrification, and store N and P in organic form between cash crops. Reduced tillage also keeps mycorrhizal networks intact for P. Sod-type forage crops in rotation reduce nitrate leaching and P runoff, and grass cover crops such as cereal rye capture leftover nitrate. Time N close to crop uptake. Holding most fertilizer until a PSNT, sensor or model shows need lets sidedress N be applied only if wanted.

soil-fert-258.title: Tending a compost pile: air, moisture and heat
soil-fert-258.text:
A compost pile is a living machine that must breathe. Managing one means keeping air, moisture and heat in the range where composting microbes work well ({{ref:soil-fert-029}}). Oxygen moves into a pile while carbon dioxide, moisture and heat rise out, so it must pass air yet hold heat. Bulking agents such as chips or chopped straw keep fine material open.

Settled piles are about 3-5 feet tall and 6-10 feet across at the base, wider in winter to hold warmth. Sites must be accessible yet away from watercourses, wells, flood plains and homes. Ideal moisture is about 40-60 percent, like a wrung-out sponge. At 35 percent or less ammonia escapes as gas and molds replace beneficial organisms.

Temperature is the main monitor. The most efficient range is 104-140 degrees F (40-60 C), though piles reach 170 F, and overheating kills beneficial organisms too. Turning creates a new hot center, since lower sides barely compost. Farm compost may need only one or two turns, and a pile heating uniformly needs none. Too much turning dries the pile and loses nitrogen and organic matter.

soil-fert-252.title: How much manure nitrogen a crop can use
soil-fert-252.text:
Manure nitrogen is the one manure nutrient that slips away. Its availability is the share of applied nitrogen a crop can use, and it is hard to predict because nitrogen is the most dynamic nutrient ({{ref:soil-fert-099}}). Phosphorus, potassium and most other manure nutrients stay in the soil and can be judged by soil testing, whereas manure nitrogen is easily lost with rain. University and government guidelines give nitrogen availability factors, the fertilizer-N equivalent per pound of manure N. They suit planning but are imprecise because they ignore weather.

Spring applications use manure nitrogen better than fall or winter ones, since wet northeastern winters cause losses. The type of manure matters only modestly. Prompt incorporation matters a great deal, because much ammonia is lost from manure left on the surface, especially poultry and swine manure with more ammonium and urea than ruminant manure. In the Penn State table, spring poultry manure incorporated immediately has a factor of 0.75 but only 0.15 if incorporated after more than 7 days or never.

A cover crop conserves fall and winter manure nitrogen by taking it up and returning it when terminated. Analysis separating ammonia-N from organic N, and credits for earlier applications, refine the estimate. Follow-up checks such as the pre-sidedress soil nitrate test, simulation models, remote imagery and crop sensors allow in-season correction.

soil-fert-266.title: Fixed versus adaptive nitrogen recommendations
soil-fert-266.text:
Nitrogen advice comes in two families. Fixed approaches ignore season-to-season weather, and adaptive approaches adjust with field data, sensors or models. The most common is the mass-balance approach: N uptake for a yield goal minus credits from soil organic matter, preceding crops and amendments. In humid regions yield and optimum N rate are only weakly related, so fixed methods suit drier climates but are very imprecise in humid ones.

Pre-plant nitrate and labile N tests, measured early in the season, work better in drier climates such as the Great Plains but cannot include seasonal weather. Adaptive tools fill that gap. Leaf chlorophyll meters and satellite, aerial, drone or tractor sensors assess canopy N status to guide sidedress N, and simulation models use radar rainfall and soil databases.

soil-fert-265.title: Why this year's weather changes the nitrogen a crop needs
soil-fert-265.text:
Minnesota corn trials from 2015 to 2019 gained an average of 11 bushels an acre in a quarter of cases from sidedress N. Available soil nitrogen depends on recent weather, so a crop's need for supplemental N fertilizer shifts from year to year. Mineral N rises in spring but falls in a wet spring, as leaching and denitrification exceed conversion to mineral forms ({{ref:soil-fert-173}}, {{ref:soil-fert-108}}). A drier spring leaves more.

Mineralization, leaching and denitrification vary with organic matter, amendments, soil temperature (warmer means more mineralization) and wetness. Saturated warm soils lose much N. Seedlings take up little N at first, then rapidly, so an unusually wet spring may need extra sidedress N. Dry years lower yields and N need, but a drought at pollination cannot be foreseen at sidedress time. Soil tests work well for P because plant-available P is strongly adsorbed, whereas N tests cannot give all answers.

soil-fert-254.title: How regular manure builds up phosphorus and potassium
soil-fert-254.text:
Manure is not unbalanced; the trouble lies in nitrogen losses. Its nutrient ratios are roughly equal to crop needs, about 2:1 nitrogen to phosphorus. Buildup arises when nitrogen losses ({{ref:soil-fert-252}}) force high rates, so phosphorus and potassium accumulate in soil. Conserving nitrogen through timing, injection or incorporation lowers the manure rate needed, cutting P and K accumulation and the fertilizer N needed where P limits manure rates.

After many years the soil test P and K can reach excessive levels, and all solutions need lower fertilizer P and P-containing amendments. Erosion of P-rich topsoil carries sediment and phosphorus to streams and lakes. Remedies include exporting manure and using N fertilizer or legumes, spreading manure more evenly across fields, rotating to alfalfa, which draws phosphorus down, soil conservation to trap sediment, or sending manure to a neighbor or composting facility.

soil-fert-274.title: Managing soils overloaded with phosphorus
soil-fert-274.text:
A survey found the average US dairy herd was fed about 25 percent more P than the National Research Council recommends. High-P soils result from excessive P fertilizer or, more often, heavy manure use ({{ref:soil-fert-254}}), and they need managing to limit phosphorus loss to water. They are common on livestock farms with limited land and imported feed, where feed nutrients exceed those exported in animal products and where manure or compost applied to meet N adds extra P. The extra supplemental P can cost thousands of dollars for a 100-cow herd and ends up as a potential pollutant.

Risk depends on context. Sites near critical water with slope, fine texture, poor structure or poor drainage need aggressive measures, while flat, grass-bordered vegetable or urban plots pose far less. First cut P in animal diets, then stop extra P by spreading manure on more land, swapping fields, or using legume covers and forages for N. Do not use a high-P source such as compost to supply N, since P builds up over the long term.

Reduce runoff and erosion with reduced tillage, contour strips, cover crops, grassed waterways and buffers. Tile drainage can still carry P, especially after heavy liquid manure. Soil-test P falls slowly once imports stop, so test every two to three years. A one-time tillage can redistribute P built up at the surface of no-till soil, followed by starter P and injected manure.

soil-fert-261.title: Composts that help plants fight disease
soil-fert-261.text:
Compost can act like a vaccine for roots and leaves. Research by Harry Hoitink and coworkers at Ohio State University showed that composts can suppress root and leaf diseases of plants. Plants become healthier because microorganisms produce plant hormones and chelates that make micronutrients more available, so they resist infection better. Beneficial organisms compete with pathogens for nutrients, consume them or produce antibiotics, and springtails and mites devour pathogen propagules.

Composts rich in biodegradable organic matter support microbes that induce systemic resistance in plants against root and leaf diseases. The effect has a limit. Composts rich in available nitrogen can stimulate phytophthora root rot, fusarium wilt and fire blight. Applying them months ahead, leaching salts or blending with low-nitrogen compost lowers the risk.

soil-fert-241.title: Manure as an asset, not waste
soil-fert-241.text: Nutrients in the manure from a 100-cow dairy may be worth more than $20,000 a year. A 100-sow farrow-to-finish operation yields about $16,000 and a 20,000-bird broiler operation about $6,000, and soil organic matter benefits may double the value. Farm manure ({{ref:soil-fert-023}}) thus has considerable economic value as a source of nutrients and organic matter. U.S. manure from 100 million cattle, 120 million hogs and 9 billion chickens holds about 23 million tons of nitrogen. After cheap fertilizer arrived post-war, manure came to be seen as waste to dispose of. It is better spread widely than concentrated in a few places.

soil-fert-245.title: What manure contains
soil-fert-245.text: Most of what an animal eats leaves as manure. Over 70% of nitrogen, 60% of phosphorus and 80% of potassium fed may be excreted, available for recycling on cropland ({{ref:soil-fert-023}}). Manure also holds calcium, magnesium, sulfur and micronutrients, and zinc deficiency is rare on soils regularly receiving it. Analyses vary widely by feed, supplements, bedding and storage, so manure should be analysed routinely. Average liquid dairy manure holds about 25 pounds N per 1,000 gallons but may be 10 or 40. About 10 tons of dairy solid manure or 4,000 gallons liquid supply 100 pounds N, while poultry needs about 4 tons or 1,500 gallons. Poultry manure is significantly higher in nitrogen and phosphorus than other types.
